A transaction aware RedisCacheManager performs puts and evictions only after the surrounding transaction commits. Limitations: Read from RedisCacheManagerBuilder.transactionAware() and the TransactionAwareCacheDecorator javadoc in Spring Framework 7.0.9.

checklist.text: Every cache has a written reason, a known staleness limit and a measured slow path it replaces.
@EnableCaching sits on its own configuration class and every cache is declared in spring.cache.cache-names.
spring.cache.redis.time-to-live is set; no cache entry lives forever.
Cache values are stored as JSON, keys keep the cache name prefix and carry a version.
The cache manager is transaction aware and writes evict entries after the commit.
Hot keys have spread expiry times and are loaded once per pod.
spring.data.redis.connect-timeout and spring.data.redis.timeout are set far below the request deadline.
A CacheErrorHandler turns cache errors into misses; the service keeps answering when Valkey is down.
Valkey has maxmemory below its container limit and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru.
Hit ratio, command latency and evicted keys are on a dashboard; cache errors raise an alert.

checklist.text: Connection budget computed: every pool times HPA maximum, surge and draining pods, plus migrations and admin, fits the user connections of each database server.
Fixed pool: maximum-pool-size equals minimum-idle, 10 or less unless measured otherwise.
connection-timeout between 2000 and 5000 ms, max-lifetime below every connection age cap, keepalive-time below network idle timeouts, leak-detection-threshold set.
spring.transaction.default-timeout and spring.jdbc.template.query-timeout set.
Runtime role has statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
Separate migration and runtime users; the runtime user cannot change the schema.
Migrations run in a Job before the rollout; the application sets spring.liquibase.enabled to false.
Every schema change reviewed as expand and contract; no rename or drop in the same release as the code change.
Transactional changesets start with SET LOCAL lock_timeout; changesets that ran are never edited.
Integration tests run the real changelog on Testcontainers with the production PostgreSQL major version.
Alerts on hikaricp.connections.pending and hikaricp.connections.timeout.
Point in time restore rehearsed in the last quarter.
The migration Job completes before the rollout starts and a failed Job stops the rollout.
The migration Job has a versioned name (or is recreated by its hook), a low backoffLimit, an activeDeadlineSeconds and a ttlSecondsAfterFinished.

One @ImportHttpServices group per downstream system, with base-url from configuration.
redirects dont-follow for calls between services, plus a status handler that rejects 3xx.
spring.http.clients connect-timeout and read-timeout set globally, tighter per group.
HTTP library chosen explicitly with spring.http.clients.imperative.factory.

Each attempt is bounded by the client; the retry timeout plus one attempt fits the caller's own timeout.
@EnableResilientMethods present whenever @Retryable or @ConcurrencyLimit is used.
Every @Retryable sets includes, maxRetries of 2 or less, multiplier, jitter and timeout.
Only one layer in the call chain retries a given dependency.

@ConcurrencyLimit with policy REJECT on the class for each downstream system, rejection mapped to 503 or 429.
Circuit breaker or rate limiter only with a written reason, using resilience4j-spring-boot4.
Fallbacks never invent business results.
Clients come from Boot builders or HTTP Service groups, with histograms on http.client.requests.

kafka-consumers.title: 6. When does a consumer commit and what if it crashes?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-consumers-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Spring Kafka sets enable.auto.commit to false unless configured and its default AckMode is BATCH, so records polled but not committed are delivered again after a crash. Limitations: Read from the Spring for Apache Kafka reference.
records.reason: No consumer runs in the example service yet.

kafka-errors.title: 7. What happens to a message that keeps failing?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-errors-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. The DefaultErrorHandler retries a failed record with FixedBackOff(0, 9) by default, skips retries for fatal exceptions such as DeserializationException. The DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer publishes to <topic>-dlt on the same partition. Limitations: Read from the Spring for Apache Kafka error handling reference.
records.reason: No listener or dead letter topic exists in the example service yet.

kafka-lag-replay.title: 8. How do I spot trouble and replay events?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-lag-replay-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. The consumer reports lag as records-lag-max. kafka-consumer-groups.sh can reset a group's offsets to a point in time with --reset-offsets --to-datetime. Limitations: Read from the Kafka 4.2 monitoring and operations documentation.
records.reason: No consumer group runs in this repository yet, so no replay is tested.

kafka-outbox-table.title: 2. How do I run the outbox without losing events?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-outbox-table-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. The Debezium outbox event router expects the columns id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type and payload. It filters out DELETE operations on the outbox table. Limitations: Read from the Debezium outbox event router documentation; no connector runs here.
records.reason: No Debezium connector or outbox table exists in the example service yet.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-outbox-table-2 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Keeping outbox rows and deleting only below a published watermark lets a new snapshot publish events again after a lost replication slot, which insert then delete in one transaction cannot. Limitations: A design rule; the replay after slot loss is not run.
records.reason: No test drops a replication slot and replays retained rows yet.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-producer-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. The Kafka 4.2 producer defaults to acks=all with idempotence enabled. A conflicting setting without explicit idempotence turns idempotence off. Limitations: Read from the Kafka 4.2 producer configuration reference.
records.reason: No producer runs against a broker in this repository yet.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-producer-2 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. In Spring Boot 4.1.1 spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled defaults to false, so the template sends no trace context until it is enabled. Limitations: Read from the spring-boot-kafka 4.1.1 configuration metadata.
records.reason: No test checks trace propagation through Kafka yet.

kafka-schemas.title: 3. How do producers and consumers agree on the event format?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-schemas-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Karapace is Apache 2.0 licensed and compatible with the Confluent Schema Registry API. Its default compatibility level is BACKWARD. Limitations: Read from the Karapace README; the default level is taken from its example output.
records.reason: No schema registry runs in this repository yet.

kafka-topics.title: 4. How should I choose topics and keys?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-topics-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. By default the outbox event router routes by aggregatetype to the topic outbox.event.<aggregatetype> and uses aggregateid as the record key, so events of one aggregate keep their order. Limitations: Read from the Debezium outbox event router documentation.
records.reason: No connector publishes outbox rows in this repository yet.

kafka-why-outbox.title: 1. Why do events get lost or sent twice?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kafka-why-outbox-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Writing the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the data and publishing it from the write-ahead log with Debezium, removes the gap where a commit succeeds and the send fails. Limitations: Reasoned from the Debezium outbox event router documentation.

kube-graceful-shutdown.title: 2. How do I stop a pod without failing requests?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kube-graceful-shutdown-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Limitations: Timings come from the source guide and the Kubernetes pod lifecycle documentation.
records.reason: Needs a cluster, a router and steady load during a rollout; no such test runs yet.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kube-probes-1 · reproduced · baseline v0.1-b1 · 2026-10-17. records.canonical: Evidence ev-kube-probes-2 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Limitations: Reasoned from the Spring Boot 4.1.1 health configuration and the Kubernetes probe documentation.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-kube-scheduled-work-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. @Scheduled with ShedLock runs a task once per trigger across replicas, using the database clock. Limitations: Taken from the ShedLock README; ShedLock is not part of baseline v0.1-b1.

preStop sleep of at least 10 s with the native sleep action.

mono-boundaries-rule.title: 2. What may services share and what must stay apart?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-boundaries-rule-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Services in one repository depend only on contracts and generated client projects, never on another service's project. Limitations: Stated as a rule. No build check enforces it in this repository yet.

mono-build-logic.title: 4. How do I keep the build the same in every service?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-build-logic-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Gradle recommends an included build named build-logic over buildSrc for convention plugins, because any change in buildSrc makes the whole build out of date; it is added with includeBuild inside pluginManagement. Limitations: Taken from the Gradle 9.8.1 best practices and composite builds documentation.

mono-catalog.title: 5. How do I keep versions in one place?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-catalog-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. An included build-logic build reads the root version catalog by importing gradle/libs.versions.toml with from(files(...)) in its settings, and convention plugins read it through VersionCatalogsExtension. Limitations: Taken from the Gradle 9.8.1 version catalog documentation, which shows the import for buildSrc.
records.reason: The example service has a catalog but no build-logic build that imports it.

mono-ci.title: 7. How should CI decide what to build?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-ci-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. A workflow skipped by a path filter leaves its required check pending and blocks the pull request, so the only required check is a gate job in a workflow that always runs. Limitations: The pending behaviour is taken from the GitHub Actions workflow syntax documentation.
records.reason: This repository has no orchestration workflow with a gate job yet.

mono-contracts.title: 3. Where do the contracts between services live?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-contracts-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Each contract lives in contracts/<service>/, is owned by the producing service, is compared with its last release in CI and is consumed through a generated client project. Limitations: The compatibility check tool is not chosen yet.

mono-one-service.title: 6. How do I build and run just one service?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-one-service-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Including a nested project by its full path creates empty parent projects; a flat name with an explicit projectDir avoids them. Limitations: Taken from the Gradle 9.8.1 best practices for structuring builds.

mono-ship.title: 8. How does each service ship on its own?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-ship-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Limitations: Stated as a rule. No multi-service image build exists here.
records.reason: The example service is a single service with one image.

mono-when.title: 1. Should our services share one repository?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-mono-when-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. One repository suits services that one team owns and changes together; separate repositories suit services with different owners or release schedules. Limitations: Engineering judgment. There is no measurement behind it.
records.reason: A recommendation about team structure; no test can prove it. The repository has no monorepo example yet.

checklist.text: The decision to keep several services in one repository is recorded in an ADR with its reason and the owning team.
No service has a project dependency on another service; services share only contracts and generated client projects.
Each service owns its database and its migration history.
libs/ holds only deliberately reusable code, never shared entities or service internals.
Each contract lives in contracts/<service>/ with the producing service as owner.
CI compares every contract with its last released version and fails on a breaking change.
Build logic lives in an included build-logic build, added with includeBuild inside pluginManagement; no buildSrc, allprojects or subprojects.
Convention plugins have their own Gradle TestKit tests.
One version catalog at gradle/libs.versions.toml, imported into build-logic.
Each service is included by a flat project name with an explicit projectDir; the root project has no sources.
One orchestration workflow that always runs ends in a gate job that is the only required check.
Each service has its own image repository, built from the repository root and its own deploy/ folder.
The same image digest is promoted between environments; releases are tagged per service.

next-caching.title: 5. What does Next.js cache and how do I refresh it?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-next-caching-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Since Next.js 15, fetch requests and GET route handlers are not cached by default; in Next.js 16 the single argument revalidateTag is deprecated; updateTag gives read your writes in Server Actions. records.canonical: Evidence ev-next-headers-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. next.config.js headers() sets response headers per path. Next.js sends x-powered-by unless poweredByHeader is false. checklist.text: Data fetching and service calls live in server components; modules that hold secrets or call the service start with import 'server-only'.
The TypeScript client types are generated from the service's OpenAPI document and CI fails when the generated file is out of date.
The browser never calls the service directly; the Next.js server calls it by its cluster name.
Login runs the OIDC code flow on the server with a maintained library; the session is an httpOnly, secure, sameSite cookie and the access token never reaches the browser.
Every Server Action and every data access function checks the user itself, not only proxy.ts.
One image is promoted across environments; no environment specific value uses the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.
Nothing that depends on the user's session is cached in a shared cache; cached reads have a tag and a lifetime.
With more than one replica, cached data uses a shared cache handler or a short lifetime per pod.
The image is built with output: 'standalone', copies only .next/standalone, .next/static and public, runs as the node user and starts with CMD ["node", "server.js"].
Probes point at a route handler that returns 200; the grace period covers the slowest request; several replicas share the Server Actions encryption key and a deploymentId.
next.config.js sets nosniff, a referrer policy, frame denial and HSTS on every path, poweredByHeader is false and a Content Security Policy is in place.
instrumentation.ts registers OpenTelemetry with the service's address in fetch.propagateContextUrls and exports to the same collector as the service.

Messages in dead letter queues are reviewed and replayed or discarded.
Every message has a messageId and consumers skip ids they already processed in the same transaction as the work.
Queues that can fill up have a maximum length and, where old work is useless, a message TTL.
The rabbitmq_prometheus plugin is scraped with alerts on growing depth, queues without consumers and dead lettered messages.

test-image.title: 8. How do I know the image really works?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-test-image-1 · reproduced · baseline v0.1-b1 · 2026-10-17. test-layers.title: 1. Where should most of my tests live?

checklist.text: Domain classes depend on no Spring type and their tests start no Spring context.
Each adapter has a slice test: @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJdbcTest for repositories, @RestClientTest for HTTP clients.
An ApplicationModules.verify() test and an ArchUnit class with the jMolecules rule for the chosen style run in the normal build.
Database tests run against Testcontainers PostgreSQL of the production major version through @ServiceConnection, never a database that runs in memory.
The real migrations run in tests, so a changeset that does not apply fails the build.
Outbound clients are built from Boot's RestClient.Builder and tested with @RestClientTest, error responses included.
Integration tests import one shared @TestConfiguration; no @DirtiesContext and no @MockitoBean in @SpringBootTest classes.
A suite starts the built image with a read-only root filesystem as a user other than root and asserts that /readyz answers 200.
CI runners have Docker for the Testcontainers and image tests.

vt-context.title: 6. Why do my logs lose the trace ID in async work?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-context-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Work handed to another thread loses MDC and the trace context unless a TaskDecorator or Micrometer context propagation carries them. Limitations: From the Micrometer context propagation documentation and the source guide.
records.reason: The example service has no async work yet.

vt-cpu-work.title: 4. Where does CPU heavy work go?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-cpu-work-1 · reproduced · baseline v0.1-b1 · 2026-10-17. With no CPU limit, -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 overrides the CPU count the JVM detects, which also sets the number of carrier threads. Result: no CPU limit, nproc 2; -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 reports Effective CPU Count: 1. Limitations: Proves the override only; the carrier count following it is from the JDK documentation.
records.environment: GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 x64 runner, Docker, images by digest from baseline v0.1-b1

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-cpu-work-2 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. A virtual thread doing CPU work holds its carrier until it blocks, so CPU heavy requests starve the others. Limitations: From JEP 444 and the source guide.
records.reason: No CPU bound workload test runs yet.

vt-downstream-limits.title: 3. How do I keep a slow service from drowning in my calls?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-downstream-limits-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. @ConcurrencyLimit, enabled by @EnableResilientMethods, caps concurrent calls through a method. Limitations: From the Spring Framework 7 resilience documentation.

vt-enable.title: 1. Should I turn on virtual threads?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-enable-1 · compiled · baseline v0.1-b1 · 2026-10-17. The example service builds and its Spring context starts with spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true. Result: io.pyahu.fixture.hexagonal.ApplicationTest: 1 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped. Limitations: Proves the setting is accepted, not that requests run on virtual threads; no test logs the request thread yet.
records.environment: GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 x64 runner, Docker, images by digest from baseline v0.1-b1

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-enable-2 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. With spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true, Spring Boot 4.1 runs web requests, @Async tasks and @Scheduled tasks on virtual threads. Limitations: From the Spring Boot 4.1 reference and configuration metadata.
records.reason: No test checks which thread handles a request or a task yet.

vt-executors.title: 5. Why does my @Async code still run on old threads?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-executors-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. A TaskExecutor bean declared by the application replaces the virtual thread executor Boot configures for @Async; spring.main.keep-alive keeps an app with no web server running. Limitations: From the Spring Boot 4.1 reference and configuration metadata.
records.reason: The example service has no @Async or @Scheduled code yet.

vt-fan-out.title: 7. How do I call two services at once with one deadline?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-fan-out-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. Waiting on each Future with one shared deadline and cancelling late tasks returns within the deadline, while a try with resources executor waits for every task on close. Limitations: From the JDK 25 ExecutorService API and the source guide.
records.reason: No fan out test runs yet.

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-pinning-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. On JDK 25, synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread; JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events show only native frames or class initialization. Limitations: From JEP 491 and the source guide.
records.reason: No JFR recording runs under load yet.

vt-resource-limits.title: 2. Why did latency get worse after I turned them on?

records.canonical: Evidence ev-vt-resource-limits-1 · not exercised · baseline v0.1-b1. With virtual threads, a HikariCP pool sized from the database budget with a 3 second connection timeout keeps tail latency bounded under load. Limitations: Reasoned from HikariCP behaviour and the source guide; server.tomcat.threads.max having no effect is from Boot's property description.
records.reason: The example service has no database yet and no load test runs.

checklist.text: spring.threads.virtual.enabled is true only for I/O bound services; the decision is recorded.
HikariCP maximum-pool-size comes from the database connection budget; connection-timeout is 5 s or less.
Every downstream service has a concurrency limit (@ConcurrencyLimit, Semaphore or bulkhead) and every outbound call has connect and read timeouts.
CPU heavy work runs on a platform pool sized to the cores.
Pod CPU request of at least 1; either -XX:ActiveProcessorCount of at least 2 with no CPU limit or a CPU limit of at least 2.
No custom executor bean silently replaces the virtual thread @Async executor; spring.main.keep-alive is true for apps without a web server.
MDC, security and trace context are propagated across async boundaries; no business logic relies on ThreadLocal caching.
Fan out uses a long lived, context wrapped executor and cancels the tasks that miss the deadline.
A JFR pinning check runs once under load; dashboards show pool pending connections and GC.
